Abstract

We study how large language models represent persistent user context across sessions when that context is supplied through retrieval rather than fine-tuning. Prior work has focused on recall accuracy in single-turn settings [3, 7], leaving open whether retrieved fragments interfere with reasoning over the primary task (Chen et al., 2024). We introduce a benchmark of 4,200 multi-session dialogues in which a small number of salient facts must be surfaced at the right moment and suppressed otherwise. Across five model families we find that precision, not recall, dominates downstream task quality: a single irrelevant fragment reduces task accuracy by 6.1 points on average, while a missed relevant fragment reduces it by only 1.4 points [12]. We further show that lexical triggers outperform dense retrieval when the cost of a false positive is high, consistent with earlier observations in information filtering (Belkin and Croft, 1992). Code and data are available at doi:10.5555/example.2026.0412.
